intro: This guide takes your group through “Watchman Nee (For Teens)” in thirteen weeks, one chapter a week. It tells the story of Ni Tuosheng, one of China’s best-known Christian teachers, the voice behind “The Normal Christian Life” and “Sit, Walk, Stand,” who spent almost twenty years in a Communist prison. The book admires him without turning him into a statue, so it also gives teens practice in thinking honestly about a flawed, gifted leader. It is written for teens aged about 13 to 18 and suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group.

Each session runs about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together. Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand if your group prefers. Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you. Do the activity, which takes about ten minutes. Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens, or nothing at all. Several chapters need care: serious illness, anxiety and depression, long imprisonment and grief, and disputed charges against Nee that include sexual immorality, which the book neither repeats as proven nor waves away. Keep to what the chapters say, and resist filling gaps with stories from elsewhere. The book also warns that teaching on brokenness and authority has been misused to control people; make clear that no leader has the right to break anyone, and that anyone being harmed should tell a safe adult. Personal reflection stays private, and if a teen seems troubled, follow up quietly afterwards.

weeks.summary: Watchman Nee was born Ni Shuzu in 1903 into a China in upheaval, where many saw Christianity as foreign because it had arrived along roads opened by Western power. He was a bright third-generation Christian who went to mission schools, yet he did not care much for the faith he had inherited. Later he took the name Ni Tuosheng, which called to mind a night watchman’s clapper, because he wanted to wake sleeping people. The big idea: faith cannot be inherited secondhand; at some point what was borrowed has to become your own.

memory_verse.text: Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me.

activity.title: Borrowed or Mine?
steps: Each person writes down privately three things they believe about God.
Next to each, write where it came from: a parent, a church, a friend, the Bible, their own experience.
As a group, talk about why receiving faith from family is a privilege, and why Nee found it was still not enough.
Each person circles one belief and asks themselves, “Have I ever made this my own?”
Close by explaining the watchman picture: an ordinary person who stays awake and tells the truth when it matters.

weeks.summary: In 1920 the Chinese evangelist Dora Yu preached, Nee’s mother renewed her faith and, as the family tells it, apologised to her son. Nee saw that following Jesus meant giving up control of his gifts and future, and when he surrendered he began putting right old wrongs. He also gave up his relationship with Charity Chang, who did not yet share his faith, not knowing whether it would ever return. The big idea: you are not your own, because you were bought with a price, and surrender is an answer to love, not a deal with God.

memory_verse.text: You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.

activity.title: Putting It Right
steps: Read the chapter’s point that making things right is the fruit of grace, not the price of forgiveness.
As a group, brainstorm ordinary wrongs teens might put right: something borrowed and not returned, a lie that needs correcting, an apology owed.
Talk about Zacchaeus and how he went beyond feeling bad.
Each person writes privately one wrong they could put right this week, and how.
Remind everyone that if putting it right could hurt someone else, they should ask a parent or pastor first.

weeks.summary: Near Fuzhou an English missionary, Margaret Barber, became Nee’s mentor, asking searching questions about whether his work came from God or merely for God. She taught him to wait on God rather than let activity replace guidance, and that faith means trusting God’s character, not feeling confident. Through her he read many Christian writers and learned to look to God for provision, becoming a gifted interpreter of many streams. The big idea: everyone, especially gifted people, needs someone who loves them enough to say no.

memory_verse.text: They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.

activity.title: For God or From God?
steps: Explain Barber’s distinction between work done for God and work done from God.
In pairs, list good activities teens are busy with: serving at church, helping friends, study, sport.
For each, discuss how you could tell whether it is from God or just busyness.
Each person writes privately the name of one older person who is allowed to tell them the truth, or, if there is no one, a prayer asking God for such a person.
Encourage everyone to ask that person this week, “Is there anything you see in me that I should work on?”

weeks.summary: In Fuzhou, Nee and other young believers met in homes to pray, study the Bible and break bread, and revival spread among students. In 1922 and 1923 disagreements broke out among the workers, and Nee was pushed out; Barber did not take his side but pointed him to the way of the cross. The chapter is careful that this never means staying in danger or being silenced by the powerful, but that you can be right in an argument and wrong in spirit. The big idea: like Christ, we can tell the truth and still entrust our reputation to God.

memory_verse.text: When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.

activity.title: Win or Resolve?
steps: Set up two volunteers to role-play a disagreement between friends, such as who forgot to send an important message.
Let them play it once with each person trying to win, extra jabs included.
Play it again with both people asking themselves, “Do I want this sorted out, or do I just want to win?”
Ask the group what changed, and what true things still needed saying in the second version.
Talk through what this teaching does NOT mean: it never means staying in danger or keeping quiet about abuse.

weeks.summary: In his early twenties Nee became seriously ill with tuberculosis and, fearing his life would be short, wrote “The Spiritual Man,” built on the idea that a person is spirit, soul and body. The chapter says many find this map helpful but warns that the Bible uses these words in overlapping ways and that feelings and thinking are not enemies of spiritual life. Nee recovered and prayed for healing, but never taught that faithful Christians won’t get sick, and the chapter adds that anxiety and depression are not failures of faith. The big idea: facing our limits teaches us to number our days and to depend on God.

memory_verse.text: So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.

activity.title: Name It, Bring It
steps: Read the chapter’s note that anxiety and depression are not a failure of faith, and that anyone struggling should tell a safe person.
As a group, list common strong feelings: anxious, angry, lonely, jealous, discouraged, excited.
Talk about the difference between obeying a feeling blindly, pretending it isn’t there, and bringing it honestly to God.
Each person writes privately one feeling they’ve had this week and a one-sentence prayer bringing it to God.
Encourage everyone to practise naming and bringing a feeling to God each day this week.

weeks.summary: By 1928 Nee’s work was centred in Shanghai, and gatherings outsiders called the “Little Flock” spread across China, wanting no name but to be the church in their city. Ordinary believers prayed, preached and carried responsibility, and Nee wanted Chinese churches to be led and supported by Chinese believers. His fellowship with the Exclusive Brethren broke down because he would not cut himself off from other genuine Christians at the Lord’s table, yet his own movement later faced the danger of treating other Christians as second-class. The big idea: Christ is not divided, so treat other believers as brothers and sisters.

memory_verse.text: Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.

activity.title: One Body
steps: As a group, list the churches and Christian groups you know of in your town.
Next to each, write one thing you think Christ is doing through them.
Discuss the chapter’s warning that every renewal movement can become the thing it protested against.
Ask: when do we treat other churches or youth groups as competition?
Choose one church on the list to pray for by name as a group before you finish.

weeks.summary: After Charity Chang became a Christian, she and Nee married in 1934, though a relative attacked him in the press. Talks he gave on Romans 5 to 8 became “The Normal Christian Life,” teaching that the cross deals with both our guilt and our old self, and that we are to know, reckon and present ourselves to God. In “Sit, Walk, Stand” he taught that we rest in what God has done before we walk and stand, and the chapter warns that counting yourself dead to sin is not pretending pain isn’t real. The big idea: you don’t fight sin to become God’s; you fight it because you already are.

memory_verse.text: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.

activity.title: Know, Reckon, Present
steps: Explain Nee’s three words and his banking picture: counting on money that has really been deposited.
Ask the group to put “sit, walk, stand” in order and explain why getting the order wrong leads to trying to earn a seat you already have.
Each person writes Romans 6:11 on a card.
On the back, they write privately what they will do the next time they fail: read the verse, confess, thank God they still belong to him, and get up.
Encourage everyone to keep the card somewhere they will see it this week.

weeks.summary: In the early 1940s Nee became involved in a pharmaceutical business linked to his brother, partly to support Christian workers, and the Shanghai elders opposed him amid accusations about the business, his ministry and his conduct. He was shut out of public ministry for about six years, and the chapter says the sources split sharply, with no simple verdict possible. It draws lessons about keeping money clear and accountable, and about identity when a role is taken away. The big idea: we are called first to be with Jesus and only then to be sent, so we are never just the thing we do.

memory_verse.text: And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach.

activity.title: Who Tells the Story?
steps: Read the chapter’s advice to ask who is telling a disputed story, and why.
In small groups, take a simple made-up event, such as a school fundraiser where money went missing, and write a short friendly account and a short hostile account of it.
Compare the versions: what did each leave out or stress?
Talk about practical ways to keep shared money clean and clear, even a class fund.
Each person writes privately one thing they are known for, and under it: “Before I was useful to anyone, I was loved.”

weeks.summary: Nee returned to public ministry in 1948, and his preaching now centred on “the breaking of the outer man”: the natural self must be broken, like a grain of wheat, for Christ’s life to come through, as with Jacob and Peter. The chapter draws a firm line that this teaching has been badly misused, and that God’s breaking never means destroying personality, losing your conscience, obeying a leader no matter what, or suffering abuse in silence. Real brokenness makes a person more tender, teachable and honest, not more afraid. The big idea: like a grain of wheat, our self-reliance must fall and die for Christ’s life to bear fruit.

memory_verse.text: Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

activity.title: Real or Fake?
steps: Read the chapter’s list of what brokenness is NOT, and say clearly that anyone being controlled or harmed by a leader should tell a safe adult.
In small groups, write six short statements a leader might make, some healthy and some controlling.
Swap with another group and sort them into “real humility” or “misuse of brokenness,” explaining why.
Discuss the chapter’s tests: can you be talked round, change your mind and apologise?
Encourage everyone to make one apology this week without adding “but.”

weeks.summary: In 1949 the Communist Party took power and Protestant leaders were drawn into the Three-Self Patriotic Movement, whose words sounded like Nee’s own teaching but served state control. In 1950 Nee chose to return from Hong Kong to share the future of the Chinese churches, and the chapter notes he and his church also joined some patriotic demonstrations. Denunciation campaigns followed, and in April 1952 he was arrested at forty-eight. The big idea: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, and real heroes are more complicated than the posters.

memory_verse.text: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

activity.title: Same Words, Different Masters
steps: Write the words “independence,” “unity” and “patriotism” where everyone can see them.
Explain how the same words meant one thing to Nee and another to the state.
In small groups, think of good-sounding words used today by schools, brands or movements, and ask what is actually being done with them.
Read Romans 13:1 and Acts 5:29 aloud, and discuss why knowing which one applies is so hard.
Pray together by name for your country’s leaders, and for Christians under pressure from their governments.

weeks.summary: Nee waited years for trial, and in 1956 he was condemned as head of a “counterrevolutionary” group and sentenced to fifteen years, on charges including economic, political and sexual misconduct. The chapter refuses both to erase the charges and to treat them as proven, noting forced confessions on one side and serious evidence argued on the other; what is certain is that he was imprisoned in a campaign to control religious leaders. His wife Charity suffered too, and the churches carried on because ordinary believers had learned to pray and teach. The big idea: Christ, not any leader, is Lord, and we are free to ask God, “How long?”

memory_verse.text: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?

activity.title: Christ, Not Them
steps: Read Paul’s line from the chapter: “let God be found true, but every man a liar.”
As a group, discuss how the Bible tells the truth about David and Peter rather than airbrushing them.
Talk about how to respond when a respected Christian is accused: without denying everything, and without assuming the worst.
Each person writes privately the name of a Christian they admire and finishes the sentence, “My faith rests on Christ, not on them, because …”
Close by reading Psalm 13 together.

weeks.summary: Little is known of Nee’s prison years, and the chapter says the honest thing is to stop where the facts stop. He generally kept the prison rules but would not deny Christ, and while he was silenced his books spread far beyond China. His fifteen-year sentence ended in 1967 without release, his family suffered in the Cultural Revolution, and there are reports he regretted how long Charity had spent alone. The big idea: endurance is not feeling strong all the time but still belonging to Christ through the dark.

memory_verse.text: Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.

activity.title: Not Forgotten
steps: Remind the group of the chapter’s encouragement: anyone in a long, dark stretch who feels there’s no point going on should tell a safe person this week.
Read Hebrews 13:3 from the chapter: “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them.”
As a group, think of the kinds of people stuck in long, hard seasons: sick, grieving, lonely, far from home, imprisoned for their faith.
Each person writes or drafts a short note to one real person in a hard season, telling them they haven’t been forgotten.
Pray together for Christians imprisoned for their faith today.

weeks.summary: Charity died before her husband, and Nee grieved her in prison. He died in custody in Anhui on 30 May 1972, aged sixty-eight, and a short statement of faith reportedly found under his pillow simply confessed that Jesus Christ is the Son of God who died for sinners and rose again. The chapter weighs whether he was a martyr and traces his worldwide influence, then uses Paul’s picture of treasure in clay jars: value what God gave through him without pretending the vessel was flawless. The big idea: the watchman dies, but Christ remains.

memory_verse.text: But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.

activity.title: Four Lines
steps: Read the substance of Nee’s last statement of faith and notice what it leaves out: none of his famous vocabulary.
Each person writes their own statement of faith in four lines at most, with no religious jargon.
Invite volunteers to read theirs aloud if they wish.
As a group, name one thing to thank God for in Nee’s life and one place where the book says his ideas needed questioning.
Encourage everyone to keep their statement somewhere they will find it on a hard day.
